newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Analysts tip Deutsche Telekom price.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Analysts tip Deutsche Telekom price.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom's share issue next month, set to be Europe's largest-ever stock offering, could go on the block for around 25 marks a share, according to analysts' estimates published on Wednesday
The huge 15 billion mark ($9.8 billion) initial public offering (IPO) will transform the company overnight into the most heavily-weighted stock on Frankfurt's DAX index of 30 blue-chip stocks.
Analysts' reports that began to trickle out to the press on Wednesday portrayed DT as an investment with some short-term risks but one that could be quite profitable over time.
"The Telekom share represents an interesting investment opportunity for long-term and risk-conscious investors," concluded Helaba Trust in a report obtained by Reuters.
Hoping to smooth over apparent risks, DT said it would pay 1.5 billion marks in dividends for 1996 and plans to announce on Friday the amount it will pay to shareholders for 1997.

According to a report in the Evening Standard newspaper in London, Deutsche Bank, the main coordinator of DT's listing, expects the company to pay dividends totalling three billion marks for 1997. This should rise to four billion marks by the year 2000.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the investment division of Deutsche Bank AG, declined to comment on the report.
DT is expected to float around 500 million shares on stock exchanges in Germany, New York, Tokyo and Toronto with trade beginning on November 18.

The share price is expected to be set on November 17 after the conclusion of bookbuilding, the process in which bids are taken from potential investors. Bookbuilding is set to begin after October 22 with the publication of the final prospectus.

Studies by Sachsen Landesbank and investment bank Hauck Bankiers predicted Telekom would offer shares to investors in a range of 22 to 29 marks, which banks suggested would lead to an appropriate subscription price of 25 marks.

The main risks facing DT investors after the company's IPO are competition as it loses its monopoly to new market entrants, tougher regulation, its mountain of debt and investor disappointment over an expected decline in 1996 profits.
DT has said that cash flow is robust enough to allow the company to erase its debt systematically in coming years.
Deutsche Bank analysts, according to the Evening Standard report, expect DT to shave its 100 billion mark debt mountain by one third over the next four years.
But growing competition and the effects of new taxes will hit the company's profits this year.
In the first half of 1996, DT's net profit plunged 96 percent from the previous year's levels to 129 million marks. The huge fall resulted from one-off charges and allocations to reserves.
"There is the risk that over the short- and mid-term weak 1996 results could be met with disappointment when it is made known next year," Helaba said in its report.
"The DT share price could also suffer intermittently because of the large number of European telecommunications share offerings expected."
According to estimates of several banks, DT's earnings per share will not surpass 1995 levels until after 1998.
On the upside, Helaba expects DT to achieve average growth in earnings of 19 percent annually for the next five years.

It also believes that Germany's telecommunications regulations will benefit Deutsche Telekom, despite the liberal orientation of the new rules, so that DT will still have around 90 percent market share in the year 2000.
